column3: A believing subgroup marks a possible break from a followed course, but only indirectly bears on 8:5.
Disciplined disputation offers a parallel frame for argument, without the departure or reluctance in 8:5.
Links al-haqq with a turn away from it; it does not add the house-to-exposure movement.
A targeted bringing-out of believers supplies a close parallel for divinely directed extraction, with a protective outcome.
Direct continuation: dispute over al-haqq after it is clear is experienced as a visible deathward drive.
Separation of people at the Hour is a distinct setting from the reluctant believing group in 8:5.
A subgroup conceals al-haqq despite knowing it; this is a contrary response rather than the departure scene.
The later battle address adds the setting of divine support for believers, but not the initial reluctance.
A call produces two contending groups, clarifying that group division can follow a shared summons.
Pairs the arrival of al-haqq with widespread dislike, closely paralleling the resistance named in 8:5.
Self-argument at final recompense shares dispute language but no local movement or believing-group tension.
Bringing a people out establishes an exit-to-liberation parallel, though its darkness-to-light frame differs.
Opposes coercing people into belief; it sharpens the distinction between reluctance and compelled faith.

A warned believing group and reversal after faith offer only a remote group-level parallel.

Two groups formed by divergent courses give a secondary parallel to the divided believing response.

Homes reorganized for worship provide a parallel to house as communal locus before deliverance.
Turning back or joining a group during battle gives a tactical counterpart to the fear in 8:5.
Evidence from the Lord and al-haqq add a general confirmation frame, not the departure dynamic.
What is disliked by the Lord is not the believers' reluctance in 8:5.

A believing group defined by shared prayer is a broad communal parallel only.
Loss of covering followed by expulsion provides a contrary vulnerability-and-removal pattern.

Use of haqq-language to press desire is a contrary speech-act pattern.

The household as a site of recitation is a distant house parallel.
Trust and protection in a family matter do not add to the focus scene.

Belief, migration, and striving supply a broad positive counterpart to leaving security for divine service.
Post-battle divergence, disobedience, and desire give a nearby pattern of strain within a believing force.

Regret at missing a gain exposes an instrumental counter-reading of participation in conflict.

The command to fight, even singly, gives a counterpoint to group hesitation.
The contrast between those who remain and those who strive gives a durable framework for differing responses to mobilization.

Plots to restrain, kill, or expel the addressee give immediate surah context for departure from home.
The two groups' positions at the encounter supply the spatial battle setting that follows the departure.
The possibility of losing courage and disputing over the matter directly clarifies the group's contested response.
The encounter is presented as an event brought to completion by God, extending the bal-haqq frame of 8:5.
Steadfastness and remembrance on meeting a force supply a practical counterpoint to the earlier fear.
The prohibition on disputing lest courage fail directly bears on the argument and weakening implied by 8:5.
Leaving homes boastfully and to be seen is a sharp contrary motive to the Lord-directed departure in 8:5.
Migration and striving identify a close positive form of believing movement away from prior security.
Belief, migration, and striving reiterate the positive counterpart to the reluctant group.
Later migrants joining the believing community add only secondary community-formation context.
Expulsion of the messenger and initiating aggression give an immediate conflict-side account of why fighting is faced.
Belief, migration, and striving form a positive parallel to costly departure for God's path.
Love of houses and other attachments is explicitly weighed against striving, clarifying one source of reluctance to leave.
The Hunayn battle scene gives a later surah parallel for believers facing military stress.
Being told to go forth yet clinging to the near life directly parallels aversion to dangerous movement.
The consequence for not going forth heightens the obligation-side of the tension in 8:5.
The command to go forth regardless of ease or burden is a close explicit counterpart to reluctant mobilization.
A nearby gain would have drawn followers, while difficult distance deters them; this sharpens the cost dimension of reluctance.
Lack of readiness to go out and being held back provides a direct contrary model of non-departure.
Internal disorder among those going out supplies a secondary reason why a group may not move as one.

Seeking leave to remain behind is a close contrary response to the summons to go forth.
Rejoicing at staying behind and refusing to go out in hardship directly parallels resistance to dangerous departure.
The exclusion of those who previously stayed behind from going out again makes non-participation a sustained group pattern.
When belief and striving are commanded, some seek permission to remain; this closely parallels reluctance at obligation.
Contentment with remaining behind provides a compact contrary posture to movement with the messenger.
The messenger and believers who strive offer a positive counterpoint to those seeking to remain behind.
Excuses and sitting back by desert Arabs add a secondary pattern of refusal to join the movement.

Those unable to find transport distinguish constrained non-participation from refusal.
Those able to contribute yet seeking leave to remain provide a sharper contrary case of avoidant withdrawal.

Migration after being wronged gives a positive departure-under-pressure parallel.

Those expelled from homes without right give a close contrary form of removal tied to worship and defense.
Migration toward the Lord supplies a concise positive departure parallel.

Scarce participation under fear supplies a secondary contrast to steadfast collective action.
Expectation that hostile forces may return clarifies enduring fear after a battle threat.
Believers' response when seeing the confederates provides a positive counterpoint to aversion at danger.
